newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodian enemies turn drinking buddies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodian enemies turn drinking buddies.

text.p: A dissident Khmer Rouge guerrilla leader and his entourage laugh and chat over a long lunch with Cambodian government soldiers and assorted bodyguards.
It is an extraordinary reunion in the dusty courtyard of a former military commander's home in the eastern city of Battambang. It would have been unimaginable two months ago.
"It is like bringing together a long lost family," says Duongdy Sovann, a stocky, good-natured bodyguard with the defence ministry. "We invited the Khmer Rouge here as friends, to drink and eat."

The lunch guests, from the Khmer Rouge faction that broke away from the hardline Maoist mainstream in August, tell Reuters they are in Cambodia's second largest city on a goodwill visit from northwest Pailin town.

"We're not negotiating. We're just spending time together," says Duongdy Sovann, holding an expensive camera he brought to document the occasion in this government-held city some 85 km (52 miles) east of the rebel base on the Thai border.

Outside the compound, which locals say was the home of former local divisional commander Prom Morinak, two Khmer Rouge soldiers interrupt their meal to answer questions about why they have joined rebel dissident Ieng Sary in seeking to end more than two decades of war.

Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot, last month broke with hardline guerrillas loyal to his former brother-in-law Pol Pot and forged a ceasefire with the coalition government.
The formerly reviled Ieng Sary, sentenced to death in absentia for his role in Cambodian genocide during the Khmer Rouge's rule of terror, was pardoned last month by King Sihanouk.
Dy Chantha, 29, says he has grown tired of communism.
"I want to become a businessman and support my family," he says, distractedly toying with a hand-held video game.
His comrade, Tid Puthea, 32, nods. Like Dy Chantha, he is dressed in high-quality civilian clothes. He also wears a nine-ruby ring.
Pailin's gem fields and timber reserves have bankrolled the Khmer Rouge's war machine in its struggle against the coalition government set up in U.N.-run elections in 1993.
The Khmer Rouge, whose 1975-79 rule left more than one million people dead, signed a peace treaty with rival groups in 1991 but later reneged on the pact.
"Pol Pot and (other hardliner leaders) Ta Mok and Son Sen came to speak in Pailin in July. Pol Pot tried to make us believe in him and said we had to fight for our nation," Tid Puthea says.
Dy Chantha says: "It made me feel upset, because I don't believe any more. Pol Pot said we had to fight against capitalism, but I saw we were making no progress in war."
The two Khmer Rouge dissidents say Pol Pot's power base is continuing to erode.
"Most of the (Pol Pot loyalists) are ready to defect," Dy Chantha says when asked about hardline Khmer Rouge radio reports of increased fighting between the guerrilla factions.
"Don't believe what you hear on the radio. It's just the propaganda of Ta Mok, Son Sen and Pol Pot," he stresses.
The two men say they have heard rebel hardliners are amassing troops around their northern stronghold of Anlong Veng, but that there have been no major offensives.

While open about the military actions, the two would not give their own ranks or the name of the commander eating lunch behind the tall fence skirting the compound. "I forget his name," Dy Chantha says.
But he warms to the subject of business in his resource-rich home town of Pailin. "I am looking forward to returning," he says.
Tid Puthea says he had no choice but to look to the future and alliances with the government troops.
"We have to go forward," he says. "If we go backward, we die."
